query: Starting from crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals, what single intervention could overcome the unresolved risk of instability during operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime? Although many physical and chemical fabrication methods have been developed, synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly understood, limiting assessment of these materials for high-temperature applications. The hypothesis should remain compatible with a multielement solid solution and the potential for catalytic performance at low noble-metal content. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to untreated nanoparticles, the application and compositional boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment with a clear failure criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The instability of crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals during operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime can be overcome by supporting the nanoparticles on a carbon material, such as graphene or carbon nanotubes, which enhances the thermal stability and prevents sintering and aggregation of the nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals
generation.intervention: Supporting the nanoparticles on a carbon material
generation.conditions: Operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime
generation.mechanism: Enhanced thermal stability and prevention of sintering and aggregation of the nanoparticles
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved stability and catalytic performance of the nanoparticles
generation.boundary: Compositional boundary: near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals; Application boundary: catalytic applications in the 773–1173 K regime
generation.uncertainty: The optimal carbon material support and the detailed mechanisms of the enhanced thermal stability and prevention of sintering and aggregation are uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the stability and catalytic performance of supported and unsupported nanoparticles in the 773–1173 K regime
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the supported nanoparticles show no improvement in stability and catalytic performance compared to the unsupported nanoparticles, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Due to the difficulties in mixing different elements with various atomic radii, oxidation states, and chemical valence as well as the chemical and physical properties, high entropy materials have great challenges to obtain specimens with a homogeneous structure. The carbothermal shock method was developed to synthesize high entropy alloy nanoparticles composed of more than five elements by a flash heating and cooling process. In addition, an aerosol droplet-mediated technique was employed to synthesize the HEA nanoparticles with atomic-level mixing of immiscible metal elements. Flame spray pyrolysis (FSP) route was also used to produce single-phase (Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn)3(O)4 quinary HEO NPs. These HEA NPs were generated during the fast heating/quenching process, which resulted in the decomposition of the metal precursors and freezing-in of the zero-valent metal atoms simultaneously. These one-step HEO NP syntheses need rapid heating at high temperatures (∼2000 K for the carbothermal shock method, ∼1100 °C for the aerosol synthesis method, and ∼1900 °C for the FSP method) in a short time. These methods have a high requirement for the equipment to achieve fast heating and cooling rate

However, performance degradation would happen if there is peeling off and aggregating of the nanoparticles due to the weak interfacial bonding between the nanoparticles and the carbon support. Moreover, for the HEO with carbon support, the high-temperature treatment during the synthesis will result in the carbothermal reduction of the oxide. To overcome these limitations, we propose a low-temperature two-step synthesis of HEO NPs by combining electrospinning, following air condition annealing. Electrospinning is an electrostatic fiber fabrication technique to produce fibers with diameters ranging from 2 nm to several micrometers using polymer solutions. This technique draws increased attention because of the wide applications of the nanofibers in the fields of biosensors, tissue engineering, drug delivery as well as the energy generation aspects. Electrospinning has been utilized to produce oxide nanoparticles, such as CuO nanoparticles that are electrospun from the precursor solution including copper acetate salt and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) polymer, and then calcinated to obtain CuO nanoparticles.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications. High-entropy alloys, containing five or even more metals, have attracted significant attentions, because of their unique chemical and physical complexity, which endow alloys with tunable features and properties such as thermal stability, superior corrosion resistance, high hardness, exceptional ductility, and superparamagnetism. A wide range of researches have revealed that the nanoparticles loading on the supports could significantly improve specific surface area and surface energy compared with the bulk materials or the nanoparticles themselves,. In addition, in industrial applications, the nanoparticles need to be dispersedly immobilized on granular supports, such as Al2O3, zeolite, and carbon materials etc., which can make the catalysts feature with tunable size, shape, and stability, enhancing the catalytic performance. Therefore, the supported high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) can be promisingly applied in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion. However, the common extreme high temperature related approaches such as arc melting and laser cladding are not suitable for supporting HEA-NPs due to the rapid growth and aggregation of nanoparticles.
